Dr. Shiva Dixit

Assistant Professor, Department of Data Science, Amity School of Integrative Sciences & Health, Amity University Haryana

I work at the meeting point of machine learning and dynamical systems: using reservoir computing to learn and predict complex dynamics, and studying how interactions shape collective behaviour in coupled oscillators and self-propelled active drops.

About

I am an Assistant Professor in the Department of Data Science, Amity School of Integrative Sciences & Health, Amity University Haryana. My research brings together machine learning, particularly reservoir computing, and nonlinear dynamics, with work ranging from synchronization and oscillation suppression in coupled oscillators to experiments on self-propelled active drops. I received my Ph.D. in Physics from the Central University of Rajasthan under Prof. Manish Dev Shrimali and was an Institute Postdoctoral Fellow at IIT Bombay from 2021 to 2023. I have published more than 20 papers in journals including Physical Review E, Chaos, Soft Matter and Europhysics Letters, and I review for Physical Review E, Soft Matter and Chaos.

Research

Machine learning and reservoir computing

Learning dynamics with echo state networks, model-free and data-driven prediction using reservoir computing, physics-informed neural networks, and physical reservoir computing.

Nonlinear and complex systems

Synchronization and control, suppression and revival of oscillations, chimera states, critical transitions in coupled systems, and collective dynamics of self-propelled 1-pentanol drops and camphor systems.

Current projects

  • Learning from real-world data

    Machine learning and reservoir computing on landslide records, patient data with blood markers, and EEG recordings.

  • Reservoir computing for complex dynamics

    Predicting the behaviour and collective states of nonlinear systems from data, without a model.

  • Higher-order coupling

    How interactions among groups of three or more units, not just pairs, change synchronization and collective behaviour.

  • Coupled map lattices

    Phase ordering and spatiotemporal patterns in networks of chaotic maps.

  • Non-smooth vehicle dynamics

    Using reservoir computing to predict the nonlinear oscillations of a jumping quarter-car model, with Masahisa Watanabe and Nirmal Punetha.

Research highlights

Machine learning

Predicting collective states with reservoir computing

A parameter-aware reservoir computer built from just two echo-state network units learns the dynamics of a whole star network of oscillators, using the network’s symmetry to keep training cheap.

Chauhan, Mandal, Dixit & Shrimali, Chaos 35, 123112 (2025)

Active matter

An active drop that senses its surroundings

In a closed Y-shaped channel, a self-propelled 1-pentanol drop picks the wider arm 80% of the time and avoids an arm holding a second drop 100% of the time: an artificial form of negative chemotaxis.

Dixit, Chotalia, Shukla, Roy & Parmananda, Soft Matter 19, 6844 (2023)

Active matter

Active disks take the shortest path

Camphor and pentanol disks moving by Marangoni forces prefer the shortest route to the sink: camphor 80% of the time in a two-path channel and 68% in a three-path one, pentanol 88% and 74%.

Khatun, Chotalia, Das, Dixit & Parmananda, PCCP 26, 25590 (2024)

Coupled oscillators

Explosive death from occasional interaction

When oscillators interact only while their mean state lies in part of phase space, oscillations die abruptly, and the oscillating and dead states coexist over a range of coupling near the transition.

Dixit, Chowdhury, Ghosh & Shrimali, EPL 133, 40003 (2021)

Show 6 more highlightsShow fewer highlights

Experiments

Regulating real circuits by switching their coupling

Experiments on coupled Chua’s circuits show that making the interaction intermittent, in time or by state, can suppress oscillations with attractive coupling or stimulate activity with repulsive coupling, giving access to everything from fixed points to chaos.

Dixit, Aravind & Parmananda, Physical Review E 106, 014203 (2022)

Coupled oscillators

New rhythms from dynamic interactions

Dynamic coupling in a network of identical oscillators produces synchronization, amplitude and oscillation death, mixed states and bistability; with spatial interaction, initial conditions decide whether the transition is first or second order.

Dixit, Chowdhury, Prasad, Ghosh & Shrimali, Chaos 31, 011105 (2021)

Coupled oscillators

Tipping points from quorum sensing

Oscillators that couple to their environment only when their amplitude crosses a threshold, as in biological quorum sensing, show an abrupt first-order transition to a steady state.

Asir, Dixit & Shrimali, Eur. Phys. J. Special Topics 230, 3211 (2021)

Control

Setting amplitude and frequency together

Combining drive–response coupling with linear augmentation lets a response oscillator lock to the driver’s frequency while its amplitude is regulated separately, shown for Stuart–Landau and Van der Pol oscillators.

Aggarwal, Dixit, Prasad & Shrimali, EPL 155, 33001 (2026)

Beyond physics

Steady harvests in an orchard

Grafting and pollination links between fruit trees, modelled as a coupled map lattice, lead to anti-synchronization: half the trees bear heavily each year, so total production stays constant despite alternate bearing.

Chauhan, Dixit, Shrimali, Sakai & Prasad, Chaos, Solitons & Fractals 181, 114639 (2024)

Beyond physics

Why relationships are unpredictable

Modelling each partner’s feeling as a complex number and adding memory of the other’s past behaviour gives multistable, aperiodic relationships whose course depends on how they start.

Chotalia, Dixit & Parmananda, Chaos 33, 113131 (2023)

In the lab

Self-propelled particles move by creating a surface-tension gradient around themselves (the Marangoni effect). Placed at a junction, a 1-pentanol drop chooses a path: it senses geometric asymmetry in the channel about 80% of the time and chemical asymmetry every time. The blue line is the drop’s tracked trajectory.

Talks and events

Featured talk · July 2024

Pathway selection by an active droplet

Gordon Research Conference on Oscillations and Dynamic Instabilities in Chemical Systems

Les Diablerets Conference Center, Switzerland · 14–19 July 2024

I presented how a self-propelled 1-pentanol drop senses its surroundings: in a Y-shaped channel it picks the wider arm 80% of the time and always avoids an arm holding a second drop. The work was published in Soft Matter (2023), and follow-up results on active disks appeared in PCCP (2024).
